A malapropism is when someone accidentally uses the wrong word in place of a similar-sounding word — and that wrong word makes the sentence ridiculous, confusing, or unintentionally funny, because it means something completely different from what was intended.

The core idea is simple: two words exist in the language. They sound alike. A person — usually by mistake — says Word A when they actually meant to say Word B. The sentence ends up meaning something strange or absurd.
The clearest way to understand it is through examples

"He is the very pineapple of politeness." The speaker meant to say pinnacle, which means "the highest point" or "the very best." Instead, they accidentally said pineapple — a fruit — because the two words sound vaguely similar. The result is nonsensical.

"She can do the flamingo." The speaker meant flamenco, the Spanish dance. A flamingo is a pink bird. Similar sounds, completely different meanings.

"For all intensive purposes, the project is done." This is one of the most common malapropisms in everyday English. The correct phrase is "for all intents and purposes." When spoken quickly, "intents and" sounds like "intensive," so many people substitute it — often without realising they are even wrong.

"Don't try to illiterate me from your memory." The intended word was obliterate, meaning to wipe out completely. Illiterate means unable to read. A sound-based mix-up, same result.

The human brain stores words partly by how they sound. When someone reaches for a word — especially an unfamiliar or formal one — the brain sometimes retrieves a similar-sounding word instead of the correct one. It is a memory glitch, not necessarily a sign of low intelligence. It happens to everyone at some point.

Mostly, yes. Malapropisms are usually honest mistakes made in speech or writing. However, writers and comedians sometimes use them deliberately to make a character seem pompous, uneducated, or clueless without knowing it. A character who confidently misuses a word while remaining unaware of the error has been a favourite comedic device in literature, theatre, and film for a very long time.

A malapropism almost always produces one of three reactions in the listener or reader: laughter, because the wrong word is so out of place; confusion, because the sentence no longer makes sense; or embarrassment, once the speaker is corrected and realises what they said.

A malapropism is not a typo, which is a written error caused by pressing the wrong key, not by confusing two words. It is also not a spoonerism, which is when you accidentally swap the opening sounds of two words — for example, saying "a blushing crow" instead of "a crushing blow." A spoonerism scrambles sounds across words; a malapropism replaces one whole word with another. They are related types of verbal slip-ups, but distinct from each other.
How to use the word "malapropism" in a sentence

"When the manager told us to 'think outside the lox,' it was an amusing malapropism — he clearly meant 'box.'"

"Her speech was full of malapropisms that kept the audience quietly laughing throughout."

"Calling the event an 'escape goat situation' instead of a 'scapegoat situation' was an accidental malapropism, but a memorable one."
A quick summary to lock it in

A malapropism = using the wrong word because it sounds like the right one. The wrong word changes the meaning, usually creating something absurd or funny. It is almost always unintentional. The plural is malapropisms, and when you spot one, you can simply say, "that's a malapropism."
